name: Tulsi (Holy Basil)
variety: Species identity; no tulsi type or cultivar specified
summary: Tulsi is Ocimum tenuiflorum, a distinct species from culinary sweet basil (O. basilicum). North Carolina Extension documents seed propagation, rapid erect growth, full-sun cultivation and culinary use; no tulsi cultivar is specified.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Ocimum tenuiflorum. North Carolina Extension lists Tulsi, Tulasi and Holy Basil as common names and notes the historical name O. sanctum. This is not an Ocimum basilicum cultivar.

cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension describes a rapidly growing, erect, multi-stemmed herb that prefers full sun and moist, well-drained soil. Its regional outdoor guidance does not establish an indoor lamp setting or hydroponic recipe.

propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed propagation and notes that the plant readily self-seeds. Exact sowing depth, germination time and temperature are not supplied in the reviewed page.

harvest.guidance: NC State Extension describes the leaves as a culinary herb, commonly cooked or used in teas. It distinguishes their spicy flavor from ordinary culinary basil; this is species-level guidance.

problems.guidance: The extension profile notes self-seeding and potential weediness outside the native range. This is a regional ecological caution, not a claim of invasive status in every location.

name: Common Fenugreek
variety: Species identity; no named cultivar specified
summary: Common fenugreek is the annual species Trigonella foenum-graecum, grown for its foliage and mature seeds. NC State describes the species, while OMAFRA adds regional Ontario field-production and harvest context; no named cultivar or hydroponic recipe is represented.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts this annual species in Fabaceae. Fenugreek, Greek clover and Greek hay are common names; no cultivar or production type is inferred.

cultivation.short: Full sun; avoid persistently wet soil
cultivation.guidance: North Carolina Extension lists full sun and good drainage. OMAFRA describes fenugreek production in Ontario at 18–27°C, in well-drained loamy soil, and notes vegetative-stage frost tolerance; these are field-crop conditions, not an indoor or hydroponic prescription.

growth.short: Erect annual with compound foliage and seed pods
growth.guidance: NC State describes an erect, rapidly growing annual about 1 ft 3 in–2 ft tall. Its oval leaflets can reach about 2 in and are hairy underneath; small flowers appear in upper leaf axils, followed by pointed pods up to 4 in long with roughly 10–20 seeds. These are species-level descriptions, not a named cultivar profile.
items: A mature plant may be recognized by its compound foliage and elongated seed pods.
The source reports summer flowering and summer-to-fall harvest context; it does not establish a fixed local calendar.

propagation.guidance: NC State and OMAFRA identify seed as a propagation route. Detailed sowing, seed handling and germination evidence is kept in the linked Seed Profile rather than duplicated in established-plant care.

harvest.short: Leaf harvest and seed production follow different schedules
harvest.guidance: NC State describes green plant parts as an herb/spice and mature seeds as a condiment. In Ontario production guidance, OMAFRA gives 30–40 days for herb harvest and 105–140 days for seed production, with earlier summer herb harvest sometimes needed to avoid flowering. These are regional crop ranges, not a universal home-garden countdown or named-cultivar promise.

problems.short: Wet soils are a documented concern
problems.guidance: NC State warns that wet soils are unsuitable. OMAFRA's limited Ontario crop observations include leafhoppers, tarnished plant bug, Alternaria leaf spot and root rot; it is a regional observation list, not a complete pest inventory or a diagnosis for an individual plant. OMAFRA notes good site selection and airflow as disease-pressure considerations.

name: Peppermint
variety: Accepted horticultural hybrid; no cultivar specified
summary: Peppermint is the accepted hybrid Mentha × piperita, distinct from spearmint (M. spicata) and from the existing broad Common Mint record. NC State documents rhizomatous spread and recommends vegetative propagation.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Mentha × piperita and gives the hybrid formula M. aquatica × M. spicata. It is not interchangeable with the species Mentha spicata or the unresolved broad Common Mint identity.

cultivation.guidance: NC State describes an upright, rhizomatous perennial that prefers rich, moist soil and partial shade in its regional context. It spreads aggressively; the source suggests container culture as a way to contain the plant, not as a hydroponic recommendation.

propagation.short: Vegetative propagation is the recommended route
propagation.guidance: NC State lists division and stem cuttings as propagation strategies and notes that the plant rarely sets seed. Use vegetative material when preserving the selected hybrid identity; the source does not establish seed-starting instructions.

harvest.short: Leaves and flowers have culinary uses
harvest.guidance: NC State lists fresh or dried leaves and flowers for teas, beverages, sauces and other uses, and reports pinching as a way to encourage bushier growth. This is species-level horticultural guidance.

problems.guidance: The extension source characterizes peppermint as an aggressive ground cover. Monitor its spread and contain it where needed; do not infer a specific Garden system compatibility from this habit.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: No cited source establishes peppermint performance in nutrient-solution hydroponics.

evidence.note: Hybrid is described as upright and rhizomatous/spreading.

summary: Torenia fournieri is the species-level identity supported for the reference name Torenia. North Carolina Extension documents seed propagation, container use, shade/part-sun conditions and pinching; a violet cultivar is not established.

pruning.guidance: NC State recommends pinching back to retain a bushier shape. The claim is species-level cultivation guidance and does not define a fixed pruning schedule.

name: Alice Sundew
summary: Drosera aliciae is an accepted South African carnivorous perennial. RHS documents fresh-seed propagation, leaf/root cuttings, wet lime-free water and full-light cultivation; no conventional hydroponic compatibility is inferred.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Drosera aliciae. RHS lists the species as a perennial carnivorous plant native to the South African Cape; this identity is separate from Cape Sundew (D. capensis).

cultivation.guidance: RHS describes cultivation under glass in full light, with medium kept continually moist to wet during the growing season using lime-free water; it advises less water standing in winter and no fertilizer. These species-specific carnivorous-plant conditions are not a nutrient-solution recipe.

propagation.short: Fresh seed and cuttings are documented
propagation.guidance: RHS recommends sowing seed as soon as ripe and notes that stored seed rapidly loses viability. Leaf cuttings in the growing season and root cuttings during dormancy are alternatives; no numeric germination schedule is reported.

problems.short: Avoid interpreting low mucilage without checking conditions
problems.guidance: SANBI describes the species as a carnivorous plant of moist conditions. Do not diagnose a problem from appearance alone; check the documented moisture and water-quality context before intervention.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Carnivorous-plant wet-media guidance does not establish recirculating hydroponic nutrient-solution suitability.

evidence.note: RHS describes a dense basal rosette and clumping/mounding habit.

spread.reason: No supported mature spread was selected.

summary: Tennessee Coneflower is the accepted species Echinacea tennesseensis, not a Tennessee-selected cultivar of E. purpurea. Kew confirms its narrow native range; University of Tennessee guidance stresses isolation from other Echinacea when maintaining seed genetic integrity.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Echinacea tennesseensis and lists the historic combination E. angustifolia var. tennesseensis as a synonym. The common name is not treated as a cultivar name.

cultivation.short: Native-range context is specific to Tennessee

propagation.short: Seed may require isolation to preserve identity
propagation.guidance: University of Tennessee Extension says seed intended to retain genetic integrity should be harvested from plants isolated from other Echinacea species. The source does not provide a germination protocol or isolation distance.

name: Micro-Tom Tomato
summary: Micro-Tom is a named miniature, determinate cultivar of Solanum lycopersicum developed by the University of Florida. It is distinct from Tiny Tim; NParks reports a very compact plant and fruiting roughly 50–60 days from sowing, while general tomato hydroponic assumptions are not inferred.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Solanum lycopersicum as the cultivated tomato species. NParks identifies Micro-Tom as a dwarf, determinate cultivar developed by the University of Florida; no claim is made that it is the same cultivar as Tiny Tim.

cultivation.guidance: NParks reports Micro-Tom growing up to about 20 cm and producing a concentrated set of fruit. UF research includes it among compact tomato cultivars studied for indoor production. This does not establish compatibility with every indoor or hydroponic system.

propagation.short: Use verified cultivar seed for the named type
propagation.guidance: The references identify Micro-Tom as a cultivar and describe a fruiting interval from seed sowing, but the selected institutional sources do not specify sowing depth, germination temperature or transplant stage. Those seed-stage fields remain unresolved.

harvest.short: NParks reports an early cultivar-specific fruiting window
harvest.guidance: NParks reports fruit production about 50–60 days from seed sowing. Keep this as a source-reported cultivar estimate; it is not a local harvest guarantee or an exact maturity standard.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: UF indoor compact-tomato research and cultivar size do not establish nutrient-solution compatibility or system-specific pod limits.

identity.short: Named commercial cultivar identity: Orange Hat
identity.guidance: Kew accepts the species Solanum lycopersicum. Baker Creek sells Orange Hat tomato seed as a named product. Its supplier page is used for product/cultivar attributes only; no breeder or formal registration claim is made.

cultivation.short: Supplier describes a 6–9 inch determinate bush
cultivation.guidance: Baker Creek describes Orange Hat as extra-dwarf, determinate and 6–9 inches tall. These are supplier-stated cultivar characteristics, not dimensions for other dwarf tomatoes or a guarantee in all environments.

propagation.short: Supplier provides a specific sowing protocol
propagation.guidance: Baker Creek instructs sowing about 1/8 inch deep and reports 7–14 day germination around 75–85°F. This is product-specific supplier guidance; use the purchased packet if its instructions differ.

harvest.guidance: Baker Creek lists 55–65 days to maturity for its Orange Hat product. This estimate is retained at product scope and should not be treated as a guaranteed indoor harvest date.

pruning.short: Heavy pruning is not advised by the supplier
pruning.guidance: Baker Creek says heavy pruning is unnecessary for this determinate cultivar and describes only light lower-leaf trimming. This is a supplier-specific recommendation, not a universal tomato rule.
